{{DISPLAYTITLE:Checking a proof again later}}
{{Technical|Lean theorem prover/System/Proof export and independent checkers}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A proof that Lean accepted today should still be checkable next year, by someone else, with other
tools. This page says what Lean keeps once it has checked a file, how a kept proof can be checked
again by Lean and by programs written independently of Lean, and why the version of Lean has to
be fixed if a check is to be repeated exactly. It ends with the work that keeps proofs usable as
Lean and its libraries change.

== What Lean keeps ==

When Lean processes a source file, it saves what the file added to Lean's environment, its table
of definitions and theorems, in a compiled file whose name ends in <code>.olean</code>. The values
are stored just as they lie in memory, so a later run can load the file directly instead of
reading it piece by piece.<ref name="refelab">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Elaboration and Compilation". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Elaboration-and-Compilation], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
A file that imports another reads its compiled form; it does not check the other file's proofs
again.

That is what makes large libraries practical, and it has a consequence. A theorem imported from a
compiled file is believed because it was checked when the compiled file was made. If something
went wrong at that moment, nothing later in the same run will notice.

== Replaying the proofs ==

The first way to check again is to replay. A tool now called <code>leanchecker</code> reads the
definitions and proofs stored in compiled files and passes them through the Lean kernel once more.
It began as a separate program, <code>lean4checker</code>; it was merged into Lean and has shipped
with every version of Lean since 4.28.0.<ref name="l4c">''lean4checker'' (README of the archived project; now distributed with Lean as <code>leanchecker</code>). [https://github.com/leanprover/lean4checker github.com/leanprover/lean4checker], consulted 13 October 2026.</ref>
With the option <code>--fresh</code> it replays everything from the start, imported files
included, which is slower.<ref name="l4c" />

Lean's guide to validating proofs says what replaying catches: faults in the way Lean manages the
Lean kernel's state, for instance when it works in parallel or handles imports, and programs that
add theorems by going around the Lean kernel. It also says what replaying does not catch. The tool
uses the same Lean kernel, and it assumes the compiled files themselves are well formed.<ref name="refval">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Validating a Lean Proof". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/ValidatingProofs], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>

== Exporting a proof ==

The second way is to take the proofs out of Lean altogether. A program called
<code>lean4export</code> writes chosen definitions and theorems, with everything they depend on,
as plain text in a documented format: one record per line, each in JSON.<ref name="l4e">''lean4export'' (README). [https://github.com/leanprover/lean4export github.com/leanprover/lean4export], consulted 13 October 2026.</ref>
A program that reads this text needs no part of Lean. It sees the proofs exactly as the Lean
kernel would, without Lean's parser, its notation or its tactics in between.

Pollack had argued for this arrangement in 1998. A proof can be checked again by a second, simple
checker for the same logic, perhaps one whose correctness has been reviewed by experts and tested
on earlier proofs; if a few such checkers become trusted, people can keep using whatever tools
they like to construct proofs in the first place.<ref name="pollack">R. Pollack, "How to believe a machine-checked proof", in Giovanni Sambin and Jan M. Smith (eds), ''Twenty Five Years of Constructive Type Theory'', Oxford University Press, 1998, chapter 11 (from p. 205); first issued as BRICS Report RS-97-18, Aarhus University, 1997. [https://doi.org/10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945 doi:10.7146/brics.v4i18.18945]</ref>

== Independent checkers ==

Several programs check Lean proofs without using the Lean kernel.

'''Lean4Lean''' is a checker written in Lean itself. Its author describes it as the first complete
checker for Lean 4 apart from the Lean kernel, which is written in C++; it runs between 20 and 50
per cent slower and can check the whole of Mathlib. Because it is written in a language in which
things can be proved, properties of the checker can be proved too, and the work has already led to
one fault in Lean's checking being found and fixed.<ref name="l4l">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean", arXiv:2403.14064, version 3, 14 September 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14064 arxiv.org/abs/2403.14064]</ref>

'''nanoda''' is a checker written in Rust that reads the files <code>lean4export</code>
writes.<ref name="nanoda">''nanoda_lib'' (README), an external type checker for Lean 4 written in Rust. [https://github.com/ammkrn/nanoda_lib github.com/ammkrn/nanoda_lib], consulted 13 October 2026.</ref>
Lean's guide names it as developed independently, and as one of the checkers its strictest
procedure can use.<ref name="refval" />

The '''Lean Kernel Arena''' is a site that presents, tests and compares checkers for Lean on a
common set of tests. When it was consulted for this page, its table listed the official checker
for Lean 4.34.1 beside Lean4Lean, nanoda and many others.<ref name="arena">''Lean Kernel Arena''. [https://arena.lean-lang.org arena.lean-lang.org], consulted 13 October 2026.</ref>
Lean's guide points to it for anyone who wants still more confidence.<ref name="refval" />

Agreement between checkers written by different people, in different languages, is evidence of a
different kind from a single check. When every one of them must accept, a fault would have to
be present in all of them at once to let a false proof through.<ref name="refval" />

== Fixing the version ==

A check can be repeated exactly only with the same version of Lean. A Lean project names the
version it uses in a one-line text file called <code>lean-toolchain</code>, kept at the top of the
project; the toolchain manager, elan, reads it and runs that version. Lean's reference advises
naming an exact version rather than a channel such as <code>stable</code>, so that people working
together use the same one and older states of a project can still be checked and
tested.<ref name="elan">''The Lean Language Reference'', version for Lean 4.34.0, section "Managing Toolchains with Elan". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan], consulted 14 October 2026.</ref>
The project this wiki records fixes its version of Lean at 4.34.1
(see [[Principia Machina/Lean transition|the move to Lean]]).

== Why proofs need upkeep ==

A proof, once checked, stays a proof in the logic it was checked in. What wears out is the
ability to run the check again with current tools.

New versions of Lean appear every month, and Mathlib, the main library of mathematics, moves
with them.<ref name="growing">Anne Baanen, Matthew R. Ballard, Johan Commelin, Bryan Gin-ge Chen, Michael Rothgang and Damiano Testa, "Growing Mathlib: maintenance of a large scale mathematical library", arXiv:2508.21593, version 2, 7 October 2025; to appear at the Conference on Intelligent Computer Mathematics (CICM) 2025. [https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21593 arxiv.org/abs/2508.21593]</ref> The authors of a 2025 paper on Mathlib's maintenance write that code written for one version of Mathlib may no longer compile
with a newer one, and that a project which falls too far behind may find it can no longer
contribute its results back.<ref name="growing" />
To soften this, a theorem that is renamed keeps its old name for a grace period of several
months, marked as out of date; anyone who uses the old name gets a warning that names the new
one.<ref name="growing" />

The move from Lean 3 to Lean 4 was a change of this kind on a large scale: it meant translating
Mathlib into the new language. Notes left during that translation numbered well over 5,000 in the summer
of 2023 and roughly 1,500 when that paper was written in 2025.<ref name="growing" />
(See [[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 1 to Lean 3|Lean 1 to Lean 3]] and
[[Lean theorem prover/History/Lean 4|Lean 4]].)

Two practices follow. Keep the exact version with the proof, so that the original check can be
repeated. And expect to revise the proof when moving it to a newer version, so that it stays
usable by new work.
